blocks.text: Ketterby's tide table was pinned inside their clubhouse door, a square of yellowed card with the hours of the sea printed on it in two columns, and someone had ringed today's line in pencil: high water at thirty-three minutes past four, eleven minutes after the counters would call roost-light. By the Gloaming the flats we meant to run on would lie under a foot of grey sea. The channels would fill first, bright as poured tin, and then the sea would come up over the mud between them in a thin sheet, without a sound. Ketterby knew it. They had flown here all their lives.

I stood at the edge of the mud in borrowed waders, the cold coming up through the rubber into the soles of my feet, and looked out over the flats the way I would have looked at a flock. Redshank were working the channel edges, jumpy, crying out at nothing. A curlew walked the far bank with its long bill going in and out of the mud like a needle through cloth. The water in the nearest channel was already moving, very slowly, a long breath drawn in from the sea, and I watched it and could not yet tell where it would go. Above the flats the sky was empty of everything but gulls. It would stay empty until someone raised a shade; I knew that, and all week I had kept looking up anyway, at the place over my head where something had flown after my shades came down, all the way up Wenlode hill, until full dark.

The day before, at the Circuit Loft, a clerk from the Court had come down the hill at half past eleven and pinned a notice beside the draw board. REGISTRATION OF PLAYERS FOR SEASON CCIII CLOSES AT NOON THIS DAY. Joan read it twice, her lips moving the second time.

I stood beside her at the public rail and watched her decide. The Ringing House was ten minutes up the hill. A substitute's fee was more than the club tin held, and there was nobody in Hobsmere who would come and stand by the mere now, not since Hamish. She looked up the hill once. Then she looked at the rail under her hands. I thought she was thinking of Lucas too, and of the one-match suspension waiting for him the day anyone found out what he was; I thought it, and I did not say it, and neither did she.

The Loft clock struck noon above the yard while the loft-master's hand was in the felt bag. He drew Eastfield for Ketterby Staithe against Hobsmere, and Joan let the hour go past her without moving. From then on we could field only our seven registered players, and one of the seven was in a chair by a window among the pines.

I knew Eastfield. For three winters I had fed them. They were the first flock every year to feel the spring coming; by the end of the season the cocks would be singing on the loft ridge in the thin sun, their throats shining green and purple, and the hens would sit in twos along the perches and peck at anything that came between them.

The Ringing was in the clubhouse, under the tide table. Joan held out her arm for the withy without being asked, and I put the plaited reed round her wrist and drew it snug, and her pulse went quick and hard against my thumb. Then I closed our copper, one ring at a time, each stamped CCIII: Joan's twenty-three, Mercy's twenty-four, Abel's twenty-five, Rhys's twenty-six, Lucas's twenty-seven, and my own seventy-one last. The eldest counter shook the brass token out of her felt bag: Hobsmere to attack the Roost at the staithe end, on its shingle bank by the sea wall; Ketterby to attack ours, out at the far end of the flats on a spit of stones. It was only luck. When the counters asked for sighted players to declare, the room was quiet, and Lucas looked at his hands.
Ketterby's Wing was a short square woman in a fisherman's gansey with salt dried white along the cuffs. She shook my hand and said she had read about Wenlode.

"So've their Tackers, Crate," Rhys said to me outside, tucking his hair under his cap. "Look at them. They stand off us like we've got the sweating fever. Nobody's walking into any cluster of ours today." He watched them jog out onto the mud, keeping their spacing as neat as fence posts, and sighed. "Shame. I was going to be magnificent."

Joan had the plan in her fist. "You'll keep your shades in your pocket till twenty past, won't you? Breath at forty, dark at forty-two. Twenty minutes and ten to walk down. And you'll not go near the water. Will you."
"No," I said.

The Loose was at eight minutes to four. Eastfield came up out of the crate in a single dark breath and turned over the flats, and the light lay low and pewter-coloured on the water in the channels, and the whole wide grey world smelled of salt and mud and weed. Ketterby's Wing raised at the Loose, herding along the seaward edge, and within the minute the extra bird was there at the flock's north-east side, over no one, the way it had been at Gosmoor and at Gadwell.
I kept my shades down and watched the birds.

At five past four two of them lifted off the top of the flock together and flew away low along the sea wall, side by side, matching each other wingbeat for wingbeat, paying no attention to anything else in the sky. A minute later two more went. Then a third pair, and that pair came back and joined the flock again for a while and then went for good. The loft-men went after them along the wall with their tins. Eastfield were pairing, as I had known they would, and there was nothing any Wing in the Fen could do about it.

At four twenty I raised my six. Within the minute the extra bird left the north-east edge and came across the whole width of the flock and settled in at my own shade's wingtip. It had come back to me, and I did not know yet what that cost.
At four twenty-two the eldest counter declared roost-light and called the counted flock: thirty-six of forty, four struck. Dorcas Ely wrote it down.
Then the tide came.

It came in up the channels first, as the card had promised, and then it came out of them and over the mud in a sheet so thin and quiet I could see the ribs of sand under it, and then I could not. Our runners went back from it step by step until all of them were up on the causeway, the old stone road that ran out along the north side of the flats to our Roost on the spit. Ketterby's runners did not go back. They knew where the hards were, the long ridges of firm sand that flood last, and they stood out on them in the middle of the water as calmly as herons, and their shades flew where they stood.

Every cluster I had planned was in the wrong place. The flock was out over the flooding flats and my people were strung along a stone road in a line, a pace and two paces apart, and a line of shades under the edge of a flock is good for nudging and nothing else. I wanted a hold. I could see the point bird and I could see its seven, five birds and two of Ketterby's shades, and I could see exactly where I would have put my six if I had had ground to put them on, and there was no ground there, only grey water moving.

And Joan was out on that causeway with the sea coming up on both sides of her. I could see her from where I stood, the withy pale on her wrist, and I saw her look down once at the water lapping the stones by her boots, and I watched the light lie along the water and the water climb the old dark stones of the causeway, one course and then the next, the weed on them lifting and spreading and floating out like hair, and I made myself look at every stone and every strand of weed and the grey light lying over all of it until my hands were steady, because she had not stepped back and so I would not either.
Ketterby were herding the flock toward our Roost on the spit. Their Tackers had planted their decoys low by its mouth. The extra bird flew at my shade's wingtip and did nothing at all.
At thirty-four minutes past four, a minute after high water, the peregrine came in off the sea.

I saw it first as a speck high over the water, a dark anchor-shape with its wings drawn half back, and I knew it before I could see it properly from the way it held the air, as if the air were a thing it owned. Then it folded. It came down the sky in one long line, wings shut tight to its body, falling faster than a stone falls, and as it fell the light caught it, the blue-grey back, the barred pale breast, the dark moustache down each cheek like a stroke of ink, and I have never seen anything so whole and so certain in all my life.

The flock saw it too. Thirty-six birds pulled into one another so hard and so fast that they became a single dark knot in the sky, a fist of birds, and every thread I was reading broke and re-made itself at once, each bird snatching at whichever seven were nearest now, and nearest changed every instant. The falcon went through the place where the flock had been. It missed. It came out underneath, threw itself up into the air again on the speed of its fall, and turned away over the sea without a backward look.
Of all the shapes in that sky, only one did not flinch. The extra bird held its place at my wingtip through the whole stoop as if no falcon had ever been made.
Then the flock burst.

It was like a handful of seed thrown out across a floor. Every bird went away from the middle at once, and the side of the flock nearest the falcon's line went hardest, landward, low over the water, straight toward the causeway. I saw the bird at the front of that burst coming at us across the flood, and I read its seven as it came: three birds, and then four, and then its nearest things were Joan's shade and Mercy's and Rhys's and Abel's, flying in a line along the causeway at my ceiling, and four shades among its seven turned it.
"Run," I said, and gave Joan the sign, and she and Mercy took it on with their arms. "To the staithe. Go."

They ran along the causeway toward the land with the sea on both sides of them, Rhys calling out his own running as he went, "Dorne down the causeway, hair untouched by the sea," and their shades ran above them, and the point bird followed its four shades for one wingbeat and two and three. And the flock came with it, because the flock was already going that way, away from the sea and the falcon and toward the shingle and the sea wall and the dark thatch of Ketterby's Roost, and that was the grain, and I had only to lean on it. The extra bird flew beside my shade, eighth nearest to the point bird as it had been at Wenlode, close enough to count and choosing not to be.

The turned bird went over the decoys Rhys and Abel had stuck in the shingle, and over Lucas crouched at the Roost mouth with his hands flat on the stones, and in under the thatch, and the birds behind it went after it out of the open air into the nearest cover there was. I watched them go in, and I counted them as they went, because that was the work: twenty-one. The other fifteen were scattered out over the water and would not come.
Eastfield would never answer that shape again this season, four shades strung along a road, and I did not mind.

At four forty the eldest counter called my Breath and I dropped all six. Ketterby's Wing worked her shades along the Roost mouth to draw our birds back out, but it was nearly dark and there had been a falcon in the sky, and not one of the twenty-one would leave the thatch. I did not raise again. At four forty-two, full dark. When I looked up, the extra bird was gone.
Twenty-one of thirty-six in Ketterby's Roost. Partial settle. Ketterby Staithe nil, Hobsmere Cutters two.

The counters cut our rings at the sea wall. The withy stayed on Joan. The Loft van stood at the top of the staithe with its lamps lit and the loft-men loading Eastfield into it crate by crate, and my drift went to the van as straight as a plumb line. Joan took my hand. She walked me up and down the staithe road in the dark, away from the water, ten minutes, talking all the way about sumps and tidal flaps and the silt that comes back in on every flood however often you dredge it, while Lucas walked behind with his watch and called the minutes. At the tenth he said, "Ten. W-we're done," and Joan let go of my hand and shook hers out, as if it had been holding a rope.

When it was done I went to the van and helped the loft-men lift the last crates. I could not help it; I had been a loft hand too long. Through the slats of the last one I could see two Eastfield birds pressed side by side in a corner, quiet, their shoulders touching.
Dorcas Ely came out of the dark and stood beside me.
"Off the record, miss," she said, very low. "Will you hear it off the record?"
"Yes," I said.

"We all see it. Every counter. We see forty-one and we swear the Counters' Forty when we're licensed, and we write forty. Today I saw thirty-seven and I wrote thirty-six." She was looking at the crate, not at me. "They tell us it's the league's luck."
"Is it?" I asked her.

"I don't know what it is. Last week I asked a colleague of mine to watch for it. She was counting Fallowby's match today, thirty miles inland. She telephoned the clubhouse at five." Dorcas took a breath. "It was over her flock from the Loose till full dark, at the north-east edge, the same as ever. And at twenty-one minutes past four it was at your wingtip. Both. The same minute, miss."
I thanked her. I meant it with my whole heart, and I think she could hear that, because she nodded once, quickly, and went back into the dark toward the clubhouse lamps without another word.

On Monday at dusk Joan and I walked to the far end of the causeway, and Pollard was waiting on his own side of it, by the gatepost with his chalk marks on it, while his roost came in over the reed in its thousands behind him, pouring down out of the pink sky in long smoking ribbons.
I told him about the pairs.

He watched the roost a long time. "Spring's in them," he said at last. "They'll go off in twos now, every match, till the equinox. A whole flock, this late, in under the thatch..." He looked up at the weather and left it there.
"Will be rare," I said. "The last weeks will be halves."
"Partial settles," he said, and chalked the gatepost, and did not look at it.
Seventeen points. We were off the bottom at last, with Pashley Carr beneath us and Tarrow Dyke one point above on eighteen, and two matches left to fly.

The landlord of the Dyke Arms had a letter waiting behind the bar, and he gave it to Joan as soon as we came in out of the cold. It was a long cream envelope with the Loft Court's seal pressed into the flap.
Joan read it standing, under the lamp. Then she read it aloud to me, flat, the way she reads the drainage board's minutes.

"'The Loft Court gives notice that it will sit at the Ringing House, Wenlode, on Thursday next, at ten in the forenoon, to inquire, upon the representation of Wenlode Sluice, whether the holding of the point bird in the match flown at the Sluice Reedbed on the Saturday last but one was within the rules as written. A. Stannard, Clerk.'"
She set it down on the bar and put her hand flat over it, the way Rhys had kept his hand over his letter, and for once she did not swear at all.
If the Court ruled the Seven a foul, the win at Wenlode would be struck from the table, our seventeen points would be fourteen with two matches to fly, and Hobsmere Cutters would be as good as down.
